Honestly, upon rewatching these movies, as decade-defining as it was to see the Avengers movies in theaters, they just don't hit the same on home release. Like they're plenty entertaining, and Infinity War is genuinely a great movie, but the payoff and subsequent downward trend of the MCU movies that directly followed this one (which has recently gotten better with additions like the last 2 Spider-Man movies and Thunderbolts) just feels a bit exhausting rewatching this one. I think this more negative approach I'm having with this rewatch stems from the anxiety of the upcoming Avengers movie being centered around my favorite comic book character of all time, Dr Doom, who is miles more powerful and methodical than a character like Thanos. As well as the MCU's portrayal of the character was, Thanos could and should never hold a candle. Before the MCU was celebrated for giving a new life and dedicated following to all the B-list characters Marvel had to settle with due to the big 3 (Spider-Man, F4, and the X-Men) being owned by Fox and Sony, there was a legacy of iconic comic heroes and villains that spanned over half a decade. And within the culture of comics, if you asked someone to name a comic book villain from Marvel Comics, 9/10 you're not going to hear Thanos, Ultron, or even Venom. They will say Dr. Doom. To the comic fan, Thanos is a nice can of RC Cola, but Doom... Doom is Coke from a glass. Despite this level of hype this character is known for, his film adaptations have been genuinely terrible, to the point of being disrespectful (I'm looking at you F4 2016). I guess the point I'm trying to make is that the luster is being lost for me in this film, along with the decisions of the past and present, which make me enjoy this film a little less and make me especially nervous for the film that, as a Doom fan, should leave me feeling excited but is instead making me feel the complete opposite way. All I ask for is a faithful adaptation of Dr. Doom in some facet, and I can die happy.

Ouais. Ok. Cool. Franchement ce film a cette note car c'est un film charnière, sinon je lui aurais mis 2 étoiles en terme de kiffe. Je n'ai ressenti aucune émotions, cela ne m'a pas fait rire et je n'étais pas ébahi ni ému. Le début est sympathique, voir Thor gros alcoolo c'est étrange, de même voir Tony Stark avec un enfant m'a surpris, mais c'est tout. Déjà je n'apprécie pas le fait de remonter le temps à l'aide de la technologique quantique. Ensuite je ne pense pas que les pierres permettent de refermer la branche d'univers créée (donc il existe trois univers distincts, le premier est celui dans lequel l'histoire se passe, le second est celui dans lequel on a prit les pierres et le dernier est celui dans lequel on a pris les pierres puis on les a restitués). Enfin Steve Rogers devrait avoir plus de 100 ans donc comment est-il en vie à la fin pour transmettre le costume et le bouclier ?? Cela étant dit c'était sympathique de revenir dans les précédents films, mais bon moi ce ne m'a pas trop touché vu que je les ai vu pour la plupart il y a moins de dix jours. Captain America est symbole et non un super-héros classique, il représente l'Amérique mais aussi la loyauté, le courage, le charisme, il est donc impersonnel et tout le monde qui est en digne peut être Captain America, c'est pour cela que je ne suis pas gêné par le fait que Steve Rogers ne soit plus Captain America à présent. D'ailleurs en parlant de dignité, j'ai trouve ça hyper classe que Steve Rogers ait pu maîtriser Mjöllnir. J'ai trop le seum que Black Widow soit morte c'est une de mes préférées. Elle aurait dû être présente pour l'une des meilleurs scènes du film : Toutes les super-héroïnes combattant côte à côte. La scène du sacrifice entre Hawkeye et Black Widow est bien je trouve et aussi un peu émouvante. Je suis pas content que Captain Marvel n'ait pas fait grand chose, je pense qu'elle peut prendre Thanos en 1v1 facile et c'est bien la seule. Dans mon classement elle est deuxième devant Wanda et derrière Doctor Strange. J'ai bien aimé aussi que l'Ancien soit présente pour défendre la Terre lorsque Loki était de mèche avec Ronan. J'apprécie le geste héroïque de Tony Stark qui fait subir à Thanos ce qu'il a fait subir à la moitié des êtres vivants. J'aime bien quand Thor et Peter se lancent dans une guerre d'egros (parce qu'ils ont tous les deux un énorme ego et qu'ils sont gros, hehehehehehehe je suis très fier et je souris bêtement derrière l'écran). Il y a une dernière question que je me pose du coup, dans l'histoire on est en 2019 ou bien 2024, ceux qui sont restés vivants ont vieillis par conséquent tous les élèves du lycée de Peter Parker sont morts parce que sinon certains auraient fini leurs études. Bon on verra bien parce que j'ai pas vu Spider-Man : Far from Home. Papa a répondu à une des mes contestations Captain America est encore vivant car il n'est plus un homme normal (ça fait sens). Bref le film ne m'a pas enthousiasmé. Après avoir réfléchi durant la nuit je compte au moins 9 univers parallèle, l'originel puis 4 paires d'univers (car les pierres ont été empruntés à des années différentes) constitué de la manière suivante : un univers dans lequel la pierre n'est plus puis un autre où la pierre n'était plus avant qu'elle ne soit restituée. Mais du coup ces univers dans lesquels rien ne semble avoir changer possède le même futur que l'original et du coup cela créer infiniment des univers parallèles. Donc maintenant on ne sait pas si nous sommes dans l'univers originel ou dans une des répliques (peut-être que je me trompe et qu'il y a une faille dans mon raisonnement). Du coup même si Rogers avait la capacité de vivre plus de 100 ans, il ne devrait pas être dans cette timeline et n'aurait pas donc pu transmettre son rôle. Vu le 06/08/2026

I was never the biggest fan of time travel movies. Sometimes they work really well (Back to the Future, Terminator 1 and 2, etc.). Sometimes they feel like a get-out-jail-free card when a story paints itself into a corner. The first half of ENDGAME feels a lot like the latter, playing as a greatest hits clip show just to remind us of the MCU's awesomeness. The back half works better in terms of emotion, especially as a close to both Steve Rogers and Tony Stark's storylines. It's the culmination of a decade's worth of buildup that we will likely never see again regardless of how DOOMSDAY or SECRET WARS turn out. " I love you 3000 ".                      "It's Been a Long, Long Time". El cierre definitivo de una era que cambió la historia del cine comercial para siempre. Después de 11 años, 22 películas y docenas de arcos argumentales entrelazados, Avengers: Endgame no solo logra estar a la altura de las colosales expectativas, sino que entrega una experiencia cinematográfica épica, nostálgica y profundamente emotiva. La película equilibra magistralmente la melancolía del duelo tras las pérdidas de Infinity War con la esperanza, la acción a escala monumental y el humor característico del UCM . El viaje en el tiempo no es solo un recurso narrativo, sino una hermosa carta de amor a toda la franquicia, permitiéndonos revivir momentos icónicos desde una nueva perspectiva antes del enfrentamiento final. El clímax y la batalla final es puro espectáculo visual y fan service ejecutado con brillantez, pero su verdadero corazón reside en las despedidas. Darle un cierre tan digno, humano y perfecto a personajes con los que crecimos — en especial a Tony Stark y Steve Rogers — es el mayor logro de los hermanos Russo. Un hito generacional que difícilmente se volverá a repetir. "Avengers... assemble." — Steve Rogers "I'm gonna need a dance raincheck."

I was curious about this movie because of a ridiculously enticing trailer that had Leonard Cohen 's " You want it Darker " playing over it. The lyrics seemed perfect for the images I was seeing on screen : "There's a lover in the story, but the story's still the same - There's a lullaby for suffering and a paradox to blame - I didn't know I had permission to murder and to maim - You want it darker ? We kill the flame." Well, I wish I had never seen that trailer. Because, truly, nothing was remotely as good as what those 2 minutes teased and suggested. [Spoilers ahead] ( Before I start - I know that this is adapted from a book, and I've seen, as always, people say that the book was better, but know that I am not aware of the differences bewteen the original story and its adaptation.) THE PLOT : Against her father's rules, Maren, 18, sneaks out of the house to join a slumber party with 3 other girls. She must go back ' before 6AM ' she says, just in case. We barely have any time to get to know any character, our protagonist included, that she bites off her friend's finger. She comes back home, bloodied, banging on the front door. Her dad, instantly, gives her a " You didn't ", confirming this wasn't a first. " You have 3 minutes to pack before we leave and the police comes ". This clearly isn't a first. Maren and her father flee, and start a new life, all over again. But soon enough, her dad disappears. Maren is left all alone with her 'issue', with, as a goodbye, a message on a cassette to listen to, and a birth certificate with her estranged Mother's name. Here starts the girl's journey to find the latter, and herself alongside. THE CAST : Probably my very first problem with this movie - None of the characters I felt invested in, and the second roles shone way more than the 2 protagonists, Maren ( Taylor Russell ) and Lee ( Timothée Chalamet ). They are lifeless, boring, unconvincing. They have about as much chemistry as water and oil do. We're somehow supposed to believe those two love each other to death in such a short time, and while I know young love can be intense, this is not what's accurately represented here. Lee and Maren are together by default , because ' they're the same '. That's all. We don't see them having any real meaningful conversations, we just see them be . Which again, would be fine if they had that spark, but they just do not. THE SFX : The very few gory scenes are very well executed and I honestly wished there would have been more. For a movie which the literal main theme is cannibalism, there is almost none of it on screen (or off, for that matter). THE SOUND : Oh man, that fucking acoustic guitar. Those damn 4 accords we keep hearing all throughout the movie just about drove me crazy. Every time a conversation ended, or an important scene did, we had those zoom outs accompanied by that guitar trying to be melancholic. Of what , exactly ? I couldn't tell you. This movie desperately tries to be mellow, bittersweet and contemplative, but it fails in all regards. It's just slow and vapid. You should have seen the face I made when I recognized Trent Reznor 's voice at one point (in what I learned was the title song). I still cannot believe this literal genius of a composer did this score. If it wasn't for (obviously) hearing his voice; I would have never associated Reznor (nor Atticus Ross) to this movie. THE CINEMATOGRAPHY : This is the only good part of this movie, the way it looks. If you look at the trailers, it is absolutely beautiful, the dialogue sounds heartfelt, the feelings of the characters seem intense, it looks so good. Sadly, when spread accross two excruciating hours and eleven minutes, the cinematography isn't going to be enough. Despite it being gorgeous, I still have some gripes with it; to me, the filming lacked any kind of dynamism - it actually does feel like a 2h music video at times. And believe me, I love contemplative films. This one just wasn't it for me. IN THE END : Bones and All seems like a failed promise. From the moment Maren meets Lee, the movie ironically goes downhill. It wants to be controversial but just doesn't go far enough, then take that back and tries throwing us off with disgusting, shocking  characters, but they're never an actual threat. It all falls short. And every time the protagonists do something reprehensible, they are excused, justified by their ' nature ' and the very quick and basic remorse Maren sometimes shows. Their personal set of morals is discussable too; as the only person we see the couple feeding on together is a gay guy that Lee kills in a cornfield (only after sex, for some reason), but when Maren discovers he was married to a woman with a kid, suddenly, she freaks out. Ok girl. In the end, what bothers me most probably is the parallel this film obviously tries to make, using cannibalism as an analogy. The poster says " You can't run from who you are ", pretty much making them being cannibals their whole identity, making it unquestionnable, while the movie itself fights tooth and nails to make them appear desperately human. Final note : 2/10 . Bones and All had -everything-, and I truly mean everything , on paper, to appeal to me. But I found nothing enjoyable aside from the visuals, and then again, not for 2+ hours. As I often say to myself, " This would have been a great 40min short ".

Träumer Kino der schönsten und seltsamsten Sorte, das vielleicht gar nicht so das großartige Werk mit Metaphern aufgeladen ist, sondern eher eine kleine sympatische Kuriosität. Bones and All würde ist ein wenig bizarr und voller Gegensätze, aber im Kern würde ich sagen, es ist eine Außenseiter-Story, wie man ein Leben lebt mit einem let's call it "Lebensstil", der als problematisch angesehen wird. Dazu gehört sowas wie, dass sobald das Leben unerträglich wird, man Gleichgesinnte findet, die einem Halt geben, das Konzept fatalistischer Liebe und natürlich ganz viele Bilder, die ein Midwest-Roadtrip so gemütlich machen, wie man ihn sich nur vorstellt. Der krasse Gegensatz ist dann natürlich der Part, wo Maren und ihre vielen Bekanntschaften Menschen essen, aber auch das wird weirdly eklig faszinierend eingefangen und wirkt gegen Ende fast schon karthatisch. So ganz konnte ich mir keinen Reim auf diesen Aspekt der Geschichte machen, aber wie gesagt ist der Film sehr laid back und hat mir eher etwas Komfort mit dem Gefühl gegeben, wenn man im Leben einsam ist und sich anders und missverstanden fühlt. In gewisser Weise ist es auch ein Coming of Age Film. Aus Marens Perspektive beginnt ihr Leben erst so richtig, als ihr Vater sie zurücklässt und sie die Welt auf eigene Faust, ohne einen Vormund, entdeckt. Sie lernt noch viele andere Menschen wie sie kennen und irgendwann wird klar, dass im ganzen Land eine Art Community existiert, die ihre Dränge unterschiedlich ausleben, aber alle versteckt vor der allgemeinen Gesellschaft leben. An der Stelle geht der Lebensstil von Maren und Lee auch perfekt mit der im Midwest geprägten Armut einher. Man kann sich nirgends niederlassen, entwickeln, ist generell misstrauisch und kann morden und rauben wie es einem beliebt, weils eh kaum jemand nachverfolgt. Am Ende ist Bones and All für mich weniger Horror oder große Metapher als einfach ein stimmungsvoller Roadtrip über Einsamkeit, das Heranwachsen und das Bedürfnis, irgendwo dazuzugehören. Nicht jede Idee geht für mich komplett auf, aber Luca Guadagnino erschafft daraus so eine eigenartige Wohlfühlmelancholie, dass ich mich in der seltsamen Perspektive von Maren und Lee total verloren habe.

Beautiful film. Luca did such a good job at balancing romance and horror, which are two polar opposites. The feeding scenes of the eaters were disgusting and incredibly gruesome, but watching it still felt warm somehow. Maybe it’s the muted colors and the strings that recurred throughout the film. My God, it was beautiful. I can’t believe I didn’t appreciate it as much before as I do now. Whatever they’re doing, killing and eating people, is morally wrong and just blatantly evil, but I can’t help but root for Maren and Lee. Whatever they had felt so calm and true, and they were really only like that with each other. ‘Di ko magets mga nagsasabing wala silang chemistry, to be honest kasi … kita niyo ba mga halikan scenes nila hahaha? I wanted the film to end when they had normal lives. They looked so happy. But the ending just made everything so much more painful to watch, andddd I’d watch it over and over again. It was so beautiful. What they had was bound to end eventually. Sabi nga nila, “Let’s be them for a while .” It wasn’t meant to last because they were pretending all along. I do wonder if they really had a choice, though. Maren actively decides not to eat people, but she eventually succumbs to it. Maybe cannibalism is intrinsic to them. Maybe they can stop for a while, eat their hands or whatnot in hopes of saving the people they love, but it all surfaces eventually, which is heartbreaking because it gets in the way of so many beautiful things. Or maybe… maybe they had a way out; they just didn’t know how. Siguro dito hindi magiging applicable ‘yong “if he wanted to, he would” hahahah. Ano ‘yun, final act of love niya ay ipinakain sarili niya para maging part siya ni Maren forever? Alam ko namang madali lang para sa kanila, well, for most of them at least, na mag move on sa mga kinakain nila, pero kung ako si Maren, ‘di talaga ako makakausad after niyan. Hay buhay talaga. What a painfully beautiful ending.

Another one for psych class. This is one of the worst films I've ever seen. The performances are mediocre, with DiCaprio's likely being the worst. The writing is incredibly juvenile, even with the plausible theory that the majority of the dialogue is filtered through the guy's warped mind. The film doesn't even look good or have an interesting aesthetic. The twist falls apart because it requires you to empathize with DiCaprio's character in the beginning, which I did not. Now, to the big problems. This film's portrayal of the mentally ill is disgusting. I understand that the facility is specifically meant to house people who've committed a violent crime, but the film was arguably still irresponsible in its perpetuation of the stereotype that all people with mental illness are scary, violent, completely irrational, and are deserving of no empathy whatsoever. There is no mention of the specific diagnosis that any patient, let alone the main character, has, which makes it impossible to understand the accuracy of the portrayals. This film was made too recently to still exhibit such an under-researched and outdated parody of what a real group of underprivileged people is like. Let's move on to another problem, the film's portrayal of both the Holocaust and the implications of Project MKUltra during the Cold War. These were both serious tragedies that I feel were not handled with appropriate sensitivity and were rather just half-baked elements seemingly thrown in for added novelty. With this film exhibiting these two themes in addition to its portrayal of extreme psychosis, there are too many things being explored and none of them are done properly. The main conspiracy is clearly supposed to be MKUltra, something that really did victimize psychiatric patients during the Cold War, and yet in the movie's cannon, it's confirmed to not be happening. I don't think this film is intentionally trying to say that MKUltra didn't happen, but it's a very strange and poorly thought-out choice that is completely at odds with the setting. This movie clearly did not have anything to say about any of the incredibly serious topics it includes, and thus has no comprehensive or unique thesis. En plus d'être visibles, elles sont trop serrées, elles contraignent la lecture d'un film qui a pourtant conscience de la force de l'ambiguïté émotionnelle qu'il pourrait produire chez le spectateur. La première mixture de réel et d'hallucination après un moment d'homogénéité apparente et intrigante finit par se soumettre aux lois physiques et se décante jusqu'à exposer clairement chacun de ses composants. Enjoyed this more on rewatch, I was better able to appreciate how the mood of the island is developed, with the soundscape being particularly impressive, with original score, licensed music, and classical music all coming together really well. Weather is also used particularly effectively to make the island feel isolating and uncomfortable; there's something about heavy rain at night that makes me really uncomfortable and I love the way that is used in this film. The star segment here is Ward C, feeling like walking into a nightmare within an already dreadful environment - it feels like those segments in Silent Hill when you go from normal world to Otherworld, everything just gets so suddenly worse and terrifying with no end in sight. Despite this being a psychological thriller with heavy emphasis on its ending, it still does very little for me compared to the build up on the island (which I really enjoyed) and other films in the ending-heavy "genre" (Memento, Prestige, Fight Club, Total Recall, etc.). It just never feels like the reveals that happen meaningfully impact or re-contextualize the earlier scenes of the film. Of course the context does literally change but it doesn't really change the emotional impacts, at least for me

The mystery constantly keeps you questioning what’s real and what isn’t, and the ending completely changes the way you look at everything that came before it. The cinematography, score, performances, and psychological tension all come together perfectly. It’s one of those movies where you immediately want to go back and watch it again just to catch everything you missed the first time. Fantastic

While it may not break new ground the way Taxi Driver, Mean Streets, and Goodfellas do, it is one of the most beautifully shot films I’ve ever seen, and I find it quite emotionally impactful. So why do you think Shutter Island hasn’t aged as well as his other works? Even Scorsese himself said he regrets being attached to it, and I think that’s wrong because it shows just how versatile the guy is. He can direct any genre to perfection.

Fairly dissatisfied with Paul Mescal’s performance in the film too, in fact I feel as though Frankie Corio even outperformed the then 26-year-old which is shocking. It also completely derailed any nuanced meaning for me because the way he acts is a causality and emotional anchor for Corio’s character, so for him to then not prevail in the role was an immediate disaster. I hope that this improves on rewatch, granted I give it a second chance, although I don’t see that being super likely.

J'ai trouvé le film très lent et il manque, selon moi, de dynamisme. Pendant une grande partie du film, j'ai eu du mal à être réellement captivé, la seule scène qui m'a vraiment marqué est la séquence finale, lorsque le père et sa fille dansent ensemble avant la fin de leurs vacances. Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

This was a movie which i didnt understand and definitely need to rewatch. Incredible acting from Mescal and Corio. Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

Aftersun is one of those films that feels incredibly simple on the surface, yet completely devastating underneath. The performances are so natural that they never feel like acting, they feel like real people, which makes the relationship between Sophie and her dad (Callum) deeply personal and relatable. That ordinary, everyday quality is what makes the film so heartbreaking, because it captures the small moments we often overlook until they become memories. Rather than relying on dramatic events, Aftersun quietly builds an emotional weight that lingers long after it ends, leaving a sense of love, loss and regret that feels painfully human.

Ok, so this took a lot of thinking, but I think I finally made sense of this film. This film made me see that you only know the version of someone that they show to you. The memories you have with or of someone are probably not actually what happened or who they truly are and felt in those moments. Our memories, especially from childhood can often have a rose coloured lense over them because at that time, you weren't aware of things in the grand scheme. You had an innocent mind because you were a kid. Most of my personal childhood memories have gaps. These gaps could have been good events or not so good events, and I'll never know because there was no camera. My siblings probably share the same memories as me, but with less or more gaps, with different details and specifics. My parents probably remember every specific and have no gaps in the memories I have from being a kid. Its like we were all there, at the same event, where we experienced the same thing, but we all probably remember it a little bit different. I probably won't remember writing this review, the same way I don't remember writing most of my reviews after a few weeks. Memory is a weird thing when you think about it. And this movie really made me think about it.

“You can live wherever you want to live. Be whoever you want to be. You have time." I used to envy people who had a documented life when they were kids, pictures and videos of them living as if it was the proof of existence. To see them through the eyes of their parents on how much they love and care enough to capture those moments, something to look back on in the future. I think it stems from my hatred and shame that every time there is an activity in school that requires baby photos, I will always be the only one worrying, for I have nothing to show. Maybe it was due to poverty? Lack of love and attention? Maybe they don’t just see the point in taking photos? Or maybe a little bit of a mix of all? It kinda felt bitter and pathetic, just a child wondering why I am the only one in the room who lacks that experience…and weirdly enough, I would find myself imagining that I am the one in other children's shoes, fantasizing about what it feels like to be in their family? Throughout the movie I just kept on thinking and reflecting about my relationship with my Papa. Initially I had this realization that I’ve never had anything that I could look back to; we barely had any pictures nor memories since we never went on vacations, went on a trip, or even simply went out. But I thought it would be an awesome thing to do so…I do think he deserves to have fun and do trivial things and see life without always being in a survival mode worrying about spending money on what seems to fit in the ‘wants’ and not ‘need’ category. I’ve spent most of my life with him, and I think personality-wise I am more like him. I might not like him as a person with some of his questionable morals and beliefs, but I could pretty much say that he was a great dad who literally did everything just so that me and my brother doesn't have to worry going on an empty stomach and even provide things that might not be grand, but it was better than having nothing. Actually, I do think that my dad is a cool person; he experienced so much hardship in life and knows a lot of skills in order to survive. I sometimes wish that I knew him better or even bonded with him with life outside of the house. Other times, I imagine what would his life be if I hadn't existed? The sole reason why I want to succeed in life, to have money, is just to spoil them and return all the hard work they've put in raising me; growing up, I think my parents value money more than anything, and I do get why, so I thought that maybe giving back with money would be the best thing they would totally appreciate—so that they could finally live the life for themselves and experience what they truly deserve: pampering their own needs and not for the sake of other people.

Much like through a foggy lens of a camera, it's a nostalgic reminiscence of that warm and fuzzy summer vacation, blissfully unaware of the realities of adult life, and the anxieties our loved ones can face. Only later on in life do we completely understand how significant these mundane interactions with our loved ones can be, how much meaning our words can have for them, and that we can understand what they once felt. Its emotional core is beautiful. It’s depiction of depression is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a movie, the final shot of Calum walking through the double doors into the night club to symbolize that his life was only ever heading in one direction after the time they spent together is soul crushing. Finally, it’s the lingering memory of a father's love that endures despite the crashing waves of loss and grief

J’en avais énormément entendu parler en bien, et certains le considèrent même comme un chef-d’œuvre. On me l’avait vraiment vendu comme un film incroyable, donc forcément, j’en attendais beaucoup. Et honnêtement, j’ai été assez déçu. Je comprend ce que dénonce le film et ce qu'il reflète de notre société et de la justice. Cependant j'ai trouvé ça long. Ce qui me gêne avec ce film c'est le côté élitiste de la communauté, comme si le fait de ne pas avoir une fin clairement expliquée rendait automatiquement le film plus intelligent. Personnellement, je trouve que ça peut vite donner une certaine prétention au film et à la manière dont il est présenté. Le fait de laisser le spectateur interpréter la fin peut être intéressant, mais ça ne signifie pas forcément que le film est meilleur ou plus intelligent. En soi, ça reste un bon film, je ne vais pas dire le contraire. Mais je pense que le principal problème, c’est que dès qu’un film sort un peu de l’ordinaire et propose quelque chose d’original, les gens ont tendance à énormément s’emballer. On lui attribue tout de suite une dimension exceptionnelle, voire de chef-d'œuvre. C'est dommage mais ça reste un bon film.

Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. Sandra Hüller livre une prestation remarquable, parvenant à transmettre une multitude d’émotions d’un simple regard. Une réalisation subtile qui nous plonge au plus près des émotions des personnages. Un très bon film.

Ok, so firstly, this was a rewatch but I realised that like I had never really written a proper review for this film and honestly I feel like I do want to write about it. Firstly, stupendously brilliant acting performances(even Snoop) which honestly has always been one of the most appreciated aspects of this film and it deserves all of it and more. The brilliance in the cinematography and post production is easy to ignore due to its subtlety but it is never truly that easy when the primary locations are literally a courtroom, a house built out of wood and snow-capped mountains which require completely different palettes as far as grading and other visual aspects are concerned. The decision to keep the digital noise makes it feel more real and provides so much more texture than what a generic grade would ever be capable of delivering. The ending is what ties this film together though and honestly is the reason why this will be regarded as a masterpiece for years to come.

From the jump this movie’s sound design and framing are next level. Just truly stunning work. As is befitting the French. They don’t do much super well but, boy, can they make movies. There’s something inherently cinematic about the French language. It lends itself to the dramatic. This movie has one of the best openings I have ever seen. Ratcheting up the tension immediately. In particular, a lingering shot on the guide dog of the half blind kid is astounding. The performances in this movie are all fantastic. Funny though, the DOG is the best actor in the movie! You love to see it. The drama brought on by the incompetence (at best) or clear corruption and railroading (at worst) of the French police is infuriating. Especially when you learn that this was inspired by a real case that the Italian police fumbled hard as hell. I love courtroom/crime dramas and this movie is a masterclass in the genre. Highly recommend.

bir köpek var filmde, hani al tüm oyunculuk ödüllerini ona ver inanılmaz iyi oynamış. Bir sabaha açılıyor film, bir aile. Anne, baba ve çocuk. Çocuğumuz görme engelli, Annemiz sahnede son derece sıcak fakat babamız öyle mesafeli ki kadraja girmeye bile yeltenmiyor. Sadece açtığı müziğin sesiyle varlığından haberdar ediyor bizi. Bu tanıtımdan sonra, bir düşüş gerçekleşiyor. Çocuğumuz evde değilken, baba pencereden düşüp ölüyor. O sırada evde bulunan tek kişi olan Anne ise ileride gerçekleşecek duruşmaların baş şüphelisi konumuna geçiyor. Daha sonra, filmimiz ilerledikçe bu düşüşü derinlemesine analiz ediyor, bir bakıma anatomisini çıkarıyor. Bu düşüş yalnızca  ölüme yol açmış bu kaza/cinayetin değil; bir aşkın, bir ailenin ve en önemlisi kişilere dair kafamızda oluşturduğumuz portrelerin de düşüşü. Onlara atfettiğimiz her bir iyi özelliğin, birlikte yaşadığımız her bir güzel anının bambaşka bir bağlamda nasıl bir silaha, korkunç bir eylemin kanıtına dönüşebileceğinin anatomisi. İşte bu film, tam olarak bununla ilgileniyor. İki saat otuz dakika boyunca filmimiz bunu anlatıyor. Gerçekte ne oldu? Aslında daha doğrusu, gerçekte ne olduğunu düşünüyorsun? Bu soru, izleyiciye düzenli olarak soruluyor ve  verdiğimiz cevaplar çoğu zaman (en azından benim verdiğim) bir öncekinden farklı oluyor. Spoiler olmayacak merak etmeyin, sadece ufak bir sahneden örnek vermek istiyorum. Bana kalırsa film başlangıçta sıkıca annemizin perspektifinden ilerliyor. Ortam onun açısından kuruluyor, onun gözlerinden şahit oluyoruz. Haliyle çoğumuz bu davada Annemin tarafını tutmuş oluyor. Sonra duruşmalar başlıyor ve bir sabah bir ses kaydı dinliyoruz. Ses kaydı bir tartışma hakkında. Önce ufak gerginlikler çıkıyor, sonra saygının sürdürüldüğü bir tartışmaya dönüyor. Fakat ne zamanki bu tartışma fiziksel şiddetin de dahil olduğu bir kavgaya dönüyor, görüntü kesiliyor ve aynı karakterlerimiz gibi sadece ses kaydıyla tanık oluyoruz geçmişe. Burada artık ne olduğunun kararı bize düşüyor. Ve o ana kadar her zaman tek bir açıya güvenmiş olan biz, kendimizi şüphe ederken buluyoruz. Film, bu tarafsız anlatımını soğuk atmosferi ve karakterlere mesafeli duruşuyla güçlendirmiş. Aynı zamanda ara ara kameranın el çekimi, handheld bir tarza geçmesiyle de sizi olan olayların içine bırakıyor. Kimi zaman kamera yaşananlara ayak uyduramıyor, sahne pozlamasında hatalara yer veriyor ve olanları olduğu gibi sergilemekte başarısız oluyor. Bu sayede anlattığı temayı da ustalıkla desteklemiş oluyor. Oyunculuklar gerçekten de efsane. Yazdığım birçok incelemede oyunculukları övüyorum, ben de bunun farkındayım. Fakat bana sorsanız en iyi oyunculuklar hangi filmdeydi diye, şüphe bile etmeden Anatomy of a Fall derdim. Sandra Hüller, kendi ana dili olmayan iki dilde konuşmasına rağmen destansı bir performans vermiş. Milo Machado-Graner unutulmaz bir oyunculuk sergilemiş. Hem çocuk oyuncu, hem görme engelli bir karakter hem de yas sürecini anlatan senaryo. Aktörümüz aleyhine olabilecek tüm durumların üstesinden ustalıkla gelmiş. Kadrodaki diğer oyuncularsa ortalamın çok üstünde performanslar vererek bu iki başrolümüzün emeğini boşa çıkarmamış. Son olarak, filmi sıkıcı bulan insanların olduğunun farkındayım. Hatta bunlardan birisi ablam. Dürüst konuşmam gerekirse beni bir an bile sıkmadı. Hatta film beni içine almakta o kadar başarılıydı ki bir sahnede karakterin sigarasından gelen dumanın benim odamda dolaştığını sandım. Zevk meselesidir diyip filmin temposu hakkındaki kararı size bırakıyorum. Benim için kusursuza çok yakın bir filmdi. Duygusal bağ kurmakta zorlanmış olsam da bunun bir sonraki izleyişimlerimde gerçekleşebileceğine hâlâ daha inanıyorum. Ayrıca, bir noktada bu duruma bilerek yapıldığını düşündüğümden çok da büyük bir problem olarak bakamıyorum. Şiddetle tavsiye ediyorum.

this film did not work for me. the social commentary only really works, i think, if you bought into it ahead of time and are actively looking for it in the text. the (uncharismatic, irritating) hypnotist's victims aren't sufficiently fleshed out to support the idea that through subtle manipulation he's dredging up murderous misanthropic desires simmering beneath the surface of our alienated modern culture. it just looks like magic brainwashing. there's the implied horror, i suppose, of the fundamental unknowability of other people and even your own self, of what you are capable of thinking and doing under the right circumstances, but i just don't think the film actually conveys that in a compelling way. the first half drags. it's repetitive and kinda boring, showing the hypnotist's "method" over and over in a way that doesn't really build up to much. the second half is more entertaining to watch, but it's both too concrete to leave much up to interpretation and too abstract to set up and resolve the mystery, such as it was, in a satisfying way. the depiction of hypnosis stretched my suspension of disbelief thin, all in service of something that wasn't terrifying enough to instinctually scare or relatable enough to evoke a more conscious, intellectual dread. the film does some interesting stuff from a technical perspective, but that wasn't enough to hook me. tbh reading through the reviews i got the impression that either i watched a different film to everyone else, or the audience is 95% film students

Cure di Kiyoshi Kurosawa non ha bisogno di alzare la voce per devastare chi guarda: si muove sottotraccia, facendosi largo con un'umiltà apparente che rende la resa finale ancora più sorprendente. Kurosawa lavora di pura sottrazione, appoggiandosi a un montaggio privo di sbavature e a interpretazioni di agghiacciante naturalezza per incollare lo spettatore allo schermo e mutarne radicalmente la prospettiva. Il vero orrore non risiede nell'ostentazione della violenza, ma nello spazio vuoto, in un gioco di luci e ombre gestito con l'autorità dei maestri. È un'opera che scava dritta nelle pulsioni più inconfessabili del nostro inconscio, lasciando un'impronta indelebile nell'immaginario di chiunque si esponga al suo sguardo. Un thriller psicologico ipnotico e viscerale, sconsigliato nelle ore notturne: la certezza che possa insinuarsi nella mente e non lasciarla più è fin troppo reale.

They don’t make sweaters like they used to. The primal urge to kill; just a flicker away. The terror of losing control and hurting the ones you love. The psychological as inseparable from the supernatural. Hypnotic, haunting, deeply unsettling. One of those movies that feels cursed to watch. Unfolds slowly, with a cold sense of inevitability. The assurance that you will snap someday; not a matter of ‘if’ but ‘when.’ The fire awakens something within you, an urge that has existed since the dawn of mankind. Maybe its influence is demonic in nature, maybe it’s baked into our DNA. A film too blackly intelligent to offer any easy answers or explanations; and besides, you know the truth anyway, don’t you? You’re just terrified to admit it to yourself. Kiyoshi Kurosawa is surely one of the best living writer-directors, a fact I am certain of even with this being my first film from him. A master of tone, pacing, storytelling; complete confidence in shot length, thematic subtlety, and a respect for the viewer to piece together information on their own. Beautiful, uneasy cinematography. Uses angles, windows, doorways, and distance to keep the viewer from the characters. You feel the urge to lean in, as if you’re an eavesdropper who just caught a glimpse of a strange conversation from across the beach. Long shots to prolong tension and deny release; to invite speculation, to sit with characters in moments of illogic and bewilderment. Koji Yakusho is one of the best living actors, full stop. He knows how to internalize his character’s emotions, convey changes in subtle ways, and go “big” and fully external when the story calls for it. Seeing him in a leading role is almost a seal of quality that the movie is going to be superb. This is not to discredit the work of his costars, whose work is on equal footing with his own, especially Masato Hagiwara, who gives one of the most skin-crawling performances I’ve ever seen in horror. As I was watching this, I didn’t want it to end. I know for a fact I’m going to rewatch this movie many times again, and I bet that I’ll get more out of it with each successive viewing. Its terrifying questions and insights into human psychology will stay with you long after the credits roll. This is unquestionably one of the greatest masterpieces in horror film history. Essential viewing. Mesmerizing.

www.fastretailing.com/eng/about/company/profile_yanai-koji.html so the film gives some nod to the fact that there's discontent within this worker despite his happy veneer throughout everything else that had transpired until that point. but does it explain what this could be or how it could come to happen? there is some interpersonal drama and we witness some cheating, but there is little if any attention paid to the structure these things exist in. when his coworker disappears and a new person shows up the next day, this just happens. the higher ups have taken care of it. and no further questions are asked. in [this one interview] yakusho says that his character sees the homeless man in the intersection and is moved by that he's the only one to really do so; but does he? this is a caricature too! and the film dupes us because we're grafted onto him. we have no choice in the operation, and it's made sure of that every step of the way. the whole thing is choreographed form the very beginning. take the tic-tac-to game, for example; there you have yakusho initially thinking it's just trash. the audience at this point is like, no! what are you doing, don't you see there's greater value there!! but then he realizes his mistake and even plays along. and this becomes a subplot of the film, of him filling out the tic-tac-to game, playing against some yet unseen opponent. and then when the game is over, he gets a thank you note for his role as such. and we get satisfaction in this because he did what we wanted him to. the film shines light on his face when his coworker's (ex?)girlfriend suddenly kisses him, but don't worry, it's just the light of the car door suddenly opening, no secondary function here. (by which i mean to say that this is specifically queuing us to receive this scene in a certain way). we get led along the whole time and then at the end there this pretense that it was all worth it but that life's tough and you just have to keep on. but what the real final shot is, it need be understood, gives the actual game away. that is, the grand city scape and the shining sun. while i'm not anti-city or anything like this, it's necessary to understand the relation to city that this film has from the point of its very inception. this is literally a propaganda piece for The Tokyo Toilet initiative -- an "urban revitalization" (we can just say gentrification, you don't have to be so coy) program masterminded by Yanai Koji, son of Uniqlo's CEO Yanai Tadashi. we can get another glimpse of this in a chance scene that happens when Yakusho comes across an older man standing in front of a developing plot. The old man asks Yakusho if he remembers what used to be here. Yakusho doesn't answer and the old man concludes, that's what it means to get old (you forget what used to be). But this is literally not true! Or, it doesn't have to be. It is not an inevitability of life that high end toilets financed by plastic industry and fast fashion will displace the perfectly functioning ones that existed before. It's not the fault of the people for forgetting, it's that there's a literal ongoing violence that makes people forget. And then part of this too can be the whole system of atomization that this is all tied up in, where people just exist as individual subjects, maybe tending to their own idiosyncratic archive, but there is no collective knowledge share -- there is no means of coming together and producing a history of what things have been like so that this knowledge can be passed down to future generations. Instead you get family heirlooms and hand-me-downs. Everything is purely familial, the film wants us to believe. Which has problems because generational wealth doesn't exist! This shit is stolen goods. And then so what, it's just too bad for people that never got a foothold to begin with? There has to be a better way. (More to come; this as to be the start of a research project; permitting everything goes alright tonight).

I solemnly swear that I am not being a contrarian by rating this low. On a technical level, this is not a bad film by any means. The cinematography is gorgeous, with very nice shot composition. I admired the crisp, tactile sound design. I liked the editing and thought the performances were solid. Everything else just didn’t do it for me, and I don’t think I’d recommend watching this film to anyone. I don’t wish to yuck anyone’s yum, but the level of praise this gets from people baffles me. A previous version of me would deride those people, but I now know better not to stoop to that. At the very least, I get why others appreciate it so much, I just can’t see the appeal in a way where I’m in the appreciator crowd, if that makes sense. Barely anything happens in this movie. You watch the protagonist go through the same loop: his work schedule, his hobbies, his habits, etc. There are minor deviations along the way that shake things up, but nothing intensely interesting, nor anything that really moves a strong narrative forward, with the exception of his niece showing up later in the film. Before you tell me I “missed the point”, I know for certain that I recognized the point of the film, I suppose I just don’t accept it. Maybe I don’t necessarily reject the point outright, I just don’t like the execution. It's two hours long, for the general message of appreciating life. For me, that’d be fine for a short film, but two hours just for that?! Watch a video about the importance of being present, then meditate for five minutes. You’ll get more value that way. “But, PolynesianSpa,” you say. “That’s the point. The fact that you cannot bear a two hour film about living in the moment shows that you are impatient and restless. You missed the point, for you do not appreciate the little things, you do not relish simplicity, nor do you revel in mundanity. You are incongruent with the essence of the film.” you lecture. Touché. I don’t jive with this movie on a personal level, that’s just not who I am. Still, usually I can enjoy things that I don’t directly relate to, if I like the execution enough. This just felt like a massive waste of time. Perhaps it was a lesson. I’ll admit it. I’m envious of the film’s protagonist. Hirayama lives a life of mediocrity, but that doesn’t seem to bother him. As a toilet cleaner, he is technically a vital part of the upkeep of civilization, yet I imagine it is a thankless job that does not pay as much as it should. Regardless, he does not stew in dissatisfaction. He makes the absolute most of what he has. Not me. I’ve been stuck in a slightly-above-minimum-wage job for too long. What exasperates my frustration with the film is that I myself don’t have even the slightest amount of dedication that Hirayama has. He has this unrelenting commitment to routine and work, despite said routine and work not really yielding much fulfillment. I am also of the belief, especially in our age of hypercapitalist exploitation, that one shouldn’t bust their ass for a boss/company that doesn’t care for them at all. Do your job and do it right, but don’t wear yourself out for the sake of the corporate fat cats who own you. Hirayama lacks revulsion for his overlords, choosing instead to focus on his duty. He’s achieved Nietzsche’s amor fati, a concept that I can’t fathom acquiescing to. He is complacent to his situation. I have become mostly complacent in my current status in life. I’ve avoided getting my driver’s license for about five years, and my job that I hate was only supposed to be for a gap year after high school — I am currently in my fourth year. Complacency is like a gift or skill to Hirayama, whilst it is a curse for me that I struggle to free myself from. Lying down and accepting my current state means not improving. Hirayama has mastered his lot in life, taking the routine by the reins. He has his routine down to a science, and has several locations where those who occupy them know him and have an established connection with him. I have close friends, sure, but not really any third spaces that I have integrated into my schedule. My life doesn’t operate like clockwork as Hirayama’s seems to. Granted, I’m not all bad. Sure, I struggle with productivity (took me FOREVER to write this review), but when it comes to being present and practicing gratitude, I am much better off than I once was. Coming out of an awful headspace in both my tween and teen years, in addition to a borderline mystical experience whilst on edibles, I’ve developed a stronger appreciation for life. I’m also going to school this fall, and am lined up to finally earn my license. I haven’t completely ditched my smartphone, but I bought a flip phone to keep as my main source of communication. My so-called "job that I hate" certainly could be worse. Still, a life like Hirayama’s is one I would not want to live. It looks peaceful, and he’s definitely much less neurotic than I am, but I’ve gained a sense of disgust for menial work. I want to do something meaningful and fulfilling. I tire of consuming slop and being bogged down by my stressful yet tedious job. I want to live well and make cool shit. All in due time, I guess. In the grand scheme of things, Perfect Days’ protagonist is like a background character. Disregarding the philosophical concept that we’re all finite meaningless blobs of flesh (tried to say that less pretentiously than the “floating rock” r/iam14andthisisdeep type shit), Hirayama especially is of little overall importance. He’ll likely leave no legacy, his contribution to society is not nonexistent but also isn’t monumental, and his life does not affect the lives of many others. He is quite inconsequential. He reminded me of my manager, who has told me on multiple occasions that his baseline goal in life is to live as a “background character”. Just be here, do what he can, and die a content man. I think that’s an admirable mindset to have, but the YOLO part of me finds it to be unrewarding. I don’t claim to practice what I preach, as I’m aware I’m often in a rut of passionless inaction, but I like to think my refusal to be totally complacent means that I have hope. There’s something here, I know it. The komorebi, the appreciation for music, the value of human connection, the attention to detail, the maintenance of plant life, and the ethereal quality of dreams. There are several moments that capture the indescribable lustre of life, along with the overwhelming experience of existence that makes you laugh and cry, much like Hirayama. I just found that all of that beauty was lost in the slog of seeing roughly the same thing over and over again with a few unexciting events in between. I was honestly begging for it to end at some point. Watching Perfect Days felt like watching someone else play Tomodachi Life . There’s a few brief glimmers of fun, but a majority of the time all that there is to see is a handful of characters idling around. I liked the scenes that featured 60s-70s music, it reminded me of car rides with my grandpa. The Japanese performance of “House of the Rising Sun” was very captivating. The tic-tac-toe game made me smile. My favourite scene was the shadow tag part, it was so sweet. Unfortunately, a few nuggets of brilliance scattered across a void of plotless dullness do not make an enjoyable film. This review ended up being more of a personal vent than a thorough overview of Perfect Days , but the movie felt so bland that I genuinely didn’t have much more to talk about. I didn’t care for this film on the first go ‘round, but would like to later. Perhaps next time, but not now.

Overall the film achieves aesthetically, very much taken from the same vein as Yasujirō Ozu. It’s a slow, slice of life view. I will say though that the film underperformed with character relations, and active modern pacing. A lot of the first hour could’ve been summed up in about 15 mins, and the protagonist wasn’t a very likable character. The story structured its pity around him by placing him in uncomfortable situations where you feel and for a modest guy, but other than that, nothing attracted me to him and he didn’t really arc. Passable, not a terrible watch but I wouldn’t come back.

Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.

On this rewatch, I find this to be much more somber. The last time I saw this, I didn’t get the implication that Hirayama was physically abused as a child. I got that he withdrew from his family and seemingly a fortune because of his father. I think I read it as his father put too much pressure on him to achieve more in life. The inclusion of Patricia Highsmith’s The Terrapin seems to suggest something darker and more tragic. It certainly colors Hirayama’s interaction with his niece and sister differently. Initially, I viewed Hirayama’s solitary, humble life as his choice. Possibly, an act of rebellion. But I see it differently now. His fixation on shadow and light feels connected to this unnamed trauma he carries. And the music, his routine, and the small connections he makes are little ways he allows light to seep into his life.

Hace tiempo tenía esta película en mi watchlist, inicialmente pensaba que sería como la de "Past Lives", y he de decir que no conecté mucho con esa película, por eso no le había dado la oportunidad. Pero apenas descubrí que el director fue Wim Wenders, me dije que obviamente la debía ver. Wim Wenders dirigió "Paris, Texas", mi película favorita, y definitivamente "Perfect Days" me dio todas las vibras. Una historia lenta, sin prisas, pero profunda. El uso de colores vivos, los escenarios, la cámara enfocando el entorno con cierta calma y sutileza... es perfecta. Por otro lado, me identifiqué totalmente con el personaje, quien disfruta las más pequeñas cosas. Sí soy, totalmente. Disfruta la música, que por cierto, qué buenos temas; toma foto de todo aquello bonito que le llama la atención; observa lo que le rodea; encuentra calma admirando los árboles; mira el paisaje y sonríe... recuerda, revive... vive tranquilo; feliz. Simplemente magnifica. "La próxima vez será la próxima vez... ahora es ahora"

This film has a lot of meaning as long as you aren't braindead by having watched many generic slop action films or expect something exciting and flashy to happen. If you can appreciate it and if it finds you at the right time, this film can hit you as hard as a truck. The best part about it is that you can interpret it in various ways depending on your own context. For me, this movie talks about being able to adapt to the changes that can come through your daily and comfortable routine life, while also reminding you to be open to accept doing things that will take you out of your comfort zone. After all, while enjoying the little moments in everyday life is nice, life doesn't make sense if you get stuck doing the same thing over and over again. Today is today and tomorrow is tomorrow, you need a balance between appreciating the little moments in your life and discovering new things. Don't be scared to do new things, and don't reject new opportunities. Be able to let go of your past and look straightforward. This movie has many symbolisms.

“agora é agora , da próxima vez é da próxima vez.” o filme é muito bonito falando sobre a beleza e leveza do cotidiano, mostra a simples mas não miserável vida que o hirayama leva e de como a felicidade não precisa vir de grandes conquistas ou eventos, mas da simples presença para viver o irrepetível. grande parte do filme eu achei senti falta dos diálogos e incômodo com o estilo monótono que o filme leva, mas depois fiz as pazes com o final super deslumbrante que eu fiquei completamente sem palavras.

No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

elegant. minimalist without ever feeling empty. this movie reminds you that life doesn’t have to be extraordinary to be meaningful. It finds poetry in repetition, in routine, in the tiny moments most of us rush past. Hirayama’s life is quiet, but never small. His worth is not measured by his job, but by the way he moves through the world. His music, his books, his plants, his photographs, the way he notices light through the trees... all of it becomes a portrait of someone fully present, even if not someone free from loneliness or regret. as an exhausted corporate girlie, this one hit a little too close to home.

15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

Enfin vu le film le plus populaire de Greta Gerwig (et mon premier film d’elle par ailleurs). Malheureusement j’ai pas été emballé par la proposition. Je trouve que ça faisait trop mélange entre un long clip musical et une publicité/vitrine géante de « luxe » quasiment. On en fait trop d’ailleurs avec la musique durant tout le film c’est tellement fatiguant qu’un moment, il y a deux pistes musicales l’une sur l’autre c’est juste insupportable. C’est dommage parce que la propagande féministe est louable mais le message est entaché de dialogues un peu trop enfantins ou un peu trop débiles à mon goût même si je pense que c’est l’univers qui veut ça. Le fond est pas si mal mais la forme délivrée est pas subtile et trop gratuite. L’humour en général dans le film est lourd et certains tacles pas très biens sentis. Margot Robbie est vraiment top après Ryan Gosling et Will Ferrell m’ont saoulé un peu je vais pas mentir. America Ferrera et Ariana Greenblatt sont sans plus pour ma part. Il y avait tout dans le film pour en faire quelque chose de réellement iconique et en faire un très bon blockbuster. Le côté monde alternatif, les côtés positifs et négatifs de Barbie avec ses stéréotypes sur le corps et l’esprit féminin, montrer qu’elle était, est et sera une figure de proue des jeunes filles mais surtout à l’avenir, une figure d’émancipation féminine dans une société patriarcale. Seulement, ça manque de justesse dans la forme du propos pour que ce soit apprécié de tous, à n’importe quel âge.

Greta Gerwig left subtlety and her serious face at the door for this one, and in the hands of a less capable cast and crew, it would probably fall apart. But what makes Barbie work is the absurdity and the cast and crew not taking things seriously. Ultimately, the issues it tackles are ridiculous one that really shouldn’t be issues anyway (equality, acceptance, etc.) and so making a movie that doesn’t take itself seriously and pokes fun at everything is the perfect way to tackle such absurdity. I think some people fell into the trap of trying to look below the surface of this movie, but with Barbie , what you see is what you get, and that is not at all a bad thing. I did have a couple issues with certain characters feeling a bit too flat and I thought the real world stuff was kinda boring, but overall I think this movie works really well and accomplishes all that it set out to do. Greta Gerwig is a really fantastic director and I very much look forward to her take on Narnia.

It has finally happened, dear reader. We have stumbled upon a movie I may find irredeemable, and you're about to find out how bitchy-catty-gay-west-coast-elitist I can get. As a child in grade school, I'd get tested every year for the gifted and talented education program (or GATE). And every year, I'd stare at these sequences of interwoven pentagons and triangles and be asked to predict what came next. To my chagrin, I was never selected and was relegated as the most gifted among the average-intelligence kids. IMAGINE MY HORROR when I find out gate was being used to identify kids with prescience! I can predict the future! I'm Special!  (i can't and im not, i had an undiagnosed anxiety disorder and adhd). I bet Special Agent Harker was in Gate.... humpf. THE MOVIE: As an avid follower of true crime myself and an outlier fan of the horror genre, I fought hard to find value in this film.  Sadly, I drew blanks here. The writing was not something I'd classify as "good" or even "serviceable". In the spirit of fairness, I'd say I think there's a nugget of a good idea here. The scene where they're testing Agent Harker for telepathy was really well done and captured the eerie "government is after all of us" vibe that I think is particularly compelling. All the rest of it fell flat. The connective tissue between the Christian faith and the deal-with-the-devil plot never held water because the viewer was never given any insight into Harkin's mother's thought process. My understanding of the Christian faith is that they would resist satan, not get into business with him. And especially not to that level.  this felt more like a creepypasta that was given a budget and distribution. I guess in the end I'll allow Harker to be special in her way as I don't have the bandwidth to  deal with any of that mess. A footnote: I was very sleepy watching this, and I did need to rewind a few times to catch some dialogue.

plot aside, but this is a pure aesthetic masterclass. Even if you find the narrative a bit mid, you cannot deny that Longlegs is an absolute art object. Osgood Perkins and DP Andrés Arochi crafted a visual nightmare that feels less like a standard horror movie and more like a meticulously curated, deeply unsettling painting. The way they weaponize the image composition is insane. Switching from those grainy, claustrophobic 4:3 35mm flashbacks to the ultra-wide 2.39:1 digital present creates this massive, yawning negative space. Arochi uses extreme wide-angle lenses even for close-ups, which slightly distorts the world and leaves so much empty air around Maika Monroe. The dread doesn't come from jumpscares but rather lives right there in the empty corners of the frame, waiting. I also loved the color palette. You're constantly trapped between the freezing, desaturated blues of the Oregon winters and the sickly, feverish ochre/orange tones leaking through the windows of the interior scenes. Then, the sudden, sharp slashes of devilish red just cut right through the monochrome sadness. It's visually rigid, perfectly symmetrical and deeply atmospheric. Even if the script didn't fully work for many, the sheer craftsmanship on display here is undeniable.

J'aime beaucoup le jeu d'acteur de Maika Monroe (Lee) dans ce film. Elle campe à merveille ce personnage d'introvertie, constamment mal dans sa peau et épuisée par l'affaire. Dès les premières scènes on voit qu'elle ne se sent pas bien, et plus ça avance, plus ça empire. Le film ne lui donne jamais de vraie catharsis, ce que j'aurais bien aimé voir, mais je suppose que c'est par choix. (Bon, il y a eu le cri dans la voiture vers la fin, mais pas assez cathartique à mon goût vu tout ce que la pauvre a vécu !) Le meilleur acte reste selon moi le premier : mention spéciale à toute la scène où Lee rentre chez elle, particulièrement réussie, exemplaire en terme de tension. On a, de plus, le droit à une photo hyper léchée (la palette de couleurs du film, les ombres et les cadrages avec ces plans larges, vraiment un plaisir pour les yeux), une bande son qui fait bien le taf (même si peu mémorable), et une belle atmosphère. Le film ne cache pas ses influences, notamment du côté de Fincher, avec Seven et Zodiac , néanmoins ça ne le dessert pas à mon sens. Mais Cage cabotine . Et ça m'emmerde que ce soit le cas. Je sais pas, c'est peut-être moi, mais je ne trouve pas les scènes avec lui particulièrement intéressantes, la faute à des répliques peu inspirées et au manque d'idées de mise en scène lorsqu'il apparaît à l'écran. Pourtant, il y avait quelque chose à faire avec un Cage qui en fait des caisses, mais là y a aucune aura, le personnage ne dit rien ou ne fait rien qui n'ait été fait ailleurs en mieux, même le maquillage est assez bof. Sa performance est clairement plombée par l'incapacité du film à lui donner des répliques et des motivations qui soient suffisamment marquées (à part le "UNMAKE MEEE!" qui était chouette) et faisant un minimum froid dans le dos. C'est là où le film pêche à mon sens le plus : il peine à faire du personnage de Cage l'entité glauque et malsaine que le mystère mérite.

GENRE ET CONSTRUCTION HISTOIRE Le film est un mélange entre enquête et un peu d'horreur par la suite, c'est étrange. L'histoire est dévoilée petit à petit, mystère après mystère. MISE EN SCÈNE On est souvent ramené de force dans l'histoire grâce à la façon dont le film est filmé. Dans la grande majorité les personages sont tes projets de la caméra. Le film partagera par moment 2 temporalités, on les reconnaît avec les couleurs : Le présent sera les couleurs grise. Pour le passé, les couleur seront plus orange chaleureuse et/ou changement de résolution de caméra (Polaroid). Lorsque le film utilisera les couleurs chaleureuse, IRONIQUEMENT l'endroit sera tous l'inverse. Le film partagera donc des couleurs diamétralement opposées, tantôt chaleureuses, tantôt glaciales, même si la grosse majorité sera plutôt grisâtre. Petit reproche tout de même pour les plans qui sont majoritairement trop sombres (normal pour un thriller MAIS lorsqu'on ne voit rien du tout, c'est un peu dommage). THRILLER Le film est angoissant et nous tient en haleine constamment (mention spéciale aux génériques de début et de fin qui ont des musiques plutôt joyeuses, étonnant pour le type de film que l'on vient de voir juste avant, j'aime bien😅). JEU D'ACTEUR Les acteurs sont vraiment bon (Maika Monroe et Nicolas Cage). CONCLUSION Bref, le film dégage une ambiance spéciale et surtout UNIQUE, je le trouve VRAIMENT TRES TRES BIEN !!!!

Maika Monroe played Agent Lee Harker with a look in her eyes that the viewer isn’t able to see through  from the beginning of the film. We can tell something haunts her, something we’re yet to see including her. Throughout the performance her character is being portrayed as “highly intuitive” but even with her intuition she never expects to keep finding herself in front of the gun. With a a new sense of terror waiting for her at each turn, or perhaps the same one that haunts her just getting louder and louder. With that being said Maika Monroe has done this role justice. Alice Witt and Nicholas Cage gave me the horror I wanted, turning this movie into something I told myself I’d be watching again without a doubt. The plot strings itself together with beautiful maddening detail, as Oz Perkins directs the hell out of it . The lack of on screen kills turns our focus to Maika and the horror she experiences throughout the film, but I’ll say the last act makes for a gruesome, satisfying, and emotional experience to make us clench our teeth for our beloved protagonist. Which includes my favorite shot in the film by far where the figure appears in the reflection as Carter closes the the door behind Harker. This made me say woah, it honestly shook me since I felt like there was a tension for something to pop up in unexpected places throughout just for this singular shot to relive that. I really liked this movie and it’s deserving ending

Longlegs is still terrifying to me on a rewatch. The opening feels like some fever-dream nightmare I somehow never had as a kid: hazy, surreal, and deeply unsettling in a way that immediately gets under your skin. Maika Monroe devours every scene, completely disappearing into an emotionally exhausting performance that feels both vulnerable and haunted. She’s phenomenal here, and the role firmly cements her as one of modern horror’s great scream queens. And Nicolas Cage is simply unmatched. There’s something so grotesque and unnerving about his performance that even his presence alone feels like a threat. Longlegs’ mostly grounded and disturbingly plausible storytelling fills nearly the entire film. It unfolds like a grim procedural wrapped in a tightening nightmare, constantly feeding you fragments of a mystery without letting you see the full bloody picture. Every frame feels ominous. Every silence feels loaded. There’s this persistent sense that you’re witnessing something you were never meant to see. Then, when those final pieces finally click into place, the mystery reveals itself with a horrifying inevitability. It’s entirely engrossing, relentlessly foreboding, and tensely scary in a way that lingers, leaving me second glancing shadows in the corner. Even knowing exactly where it’s going, Longlegs still manages to make me feel like I’m watching something I shouldn’t be. And that’s a helluva feat. 🩸
