Achei um filme interessante, mas a princípio fiquei com a sensação de que ele era um pouco raso. Eu estava esperando que algumas coisas fossem mais aprofundadas e, quando terminou, ainda senti que faltava alguma coisa. Mas é um daqueles filmes que continuam na cabeça depois dos créditos. Quanto mais eu pensava, mais percebia as coisas que ele deixa nas entrelinhas. Me chamou atenção como a mão funciona quase como uma metáfora para o vicio. Depois que os personagens experimentam aquele contato, eles passam a querer repetir a experiência cada vez mais, ignorando as possíveis consequências. Não parece ser só um filme sobre espíritos, mas também sobre dependência, impulsividade e a dificuldade de parar quando algo já tomou conta de você. Mia acaba sendo a maior prova disso. Carregando o luto pela mãe, ela se agarra à ilusão de que ainda pode falar com ela, mesmo quando fica evidente que aquilo não é realmente sua mãe. Também achei interessante como o filme trabalha os personagens. Apesar de serem um grupo de amigos, cada um mantém sua individualidade. A Mia, por exemplo, demonstra um carinho pelo Riley durante parte da história, mas, quando surge a possibilidade de conseguir algo que ela queria, ela acaba deixando esse cuidado de lado. No geral, achei uma produção bem feita, com uma boa construção dos personagens e uma atmosfera que funciona muito bem. Não foi um filme que me conquistou de imediato, mas definitivamente me fez pensar depois que terminou.

Talk to Me tem uma premissa muito boa. A ideia de uma mão misteriosa que permite conversar com espíritos é criativa e encaixa muito bem no contexto de um grupo de adolescentes que transforma aquilo em uma brincadeira de festa. O filme também tenta construir um lado mais emocional ao explorar o trauma da Mia após a morte da mãe por suicídio e como isso influencia suas escolhas. O problema é que, para mim, essa parte da história simplesmente não funciona como deveria. Todo o conflito envolvendo o Riley, as consequências de ele usar a mão e a forma como a família passa a culpar a protagonista nunca conseguiu me envolver, então o peso dramático que o roteiro tenta criar acaba se perdendo. As atuações também não ajudam muito. A Sophie Wilde entrega uma boa performance como Mia e consegue carregar boa parte do filme nas costas, mas o restante do elenco passa uma sensação de ser apenas competente, sem interpretações que realmente se destaquem. Mesmo com algumas cenas de horror bem feitas e uma atmosfera desconfortável em certos momentos, fiquei com a impressão de que a execução ficou bem abaixo do potencial da ideia. Em compensação, a maquiagem merece muito destaque. Os ferimentos, as possessões e todo o visual dos espíritos são muito bem feitos e ajudam bastante na imersão, sendo facilmente um dos pontos altos do filme. Apesar disso, o final é, sem dúvida, a melhor parte. A conclusão amarra muito bem a trajetória da Mia e as regras da própria maldição. Ver a protagonista assumindo o lugar de um dos espíritos e sendo invocada por outras pessoas fecha o ciclo de uma forma muito inteligente e dá um novo significado a tudo o que aconteceu antes. É um desfecho forte e memorável, que quase faz o filme terminar melhor do que foi durante boa parte da sua duração. Ainda assim, no geral, Talk to Me acabou sendo uma experiência apenas mediana para mim.

Holy shit, so haunting and effortlessly scary, I loved the nature surrounding the hand and the mystery behind it. The scene where Riley gets possessed gave me hella Hereditary vibes, which is a compliment btw. Both films tab into this feeling of dread and leaves you feeling unsettled beyond belief, to the point where I almost felt nauseating without being a gory mess. Something only a handful of horror movies is able to bring out in me, the sense of dread that lingers inside you throughout the film. The Philippou brother’s really made something special here, everything from the storytelling to the passing was incredible. And tremendous performance Sophie Wilde pulls in this simply can’t go unnoticed, easily the standout and lowkey carries the film acting wise! My one complaint though is with some of the characters being a little underbaked, where they feel a little pointless. Like the character of Max, who we only really see and spend time with ones, the scene where he gets stabbed, you can’t expect me to care after just two minutes of screentime! But other than that, the film feels extremely well passed, where every act and scene feels rewarding, just wished we could have seen a little more to Max… The Philippou brother’s is something else, I’ve already seen their latest film “Bring Her Back” and although I prefer this one, it’s already clear these guys mean business and I’m eagerly awaiting their next move, which I couldn’t help but notice could be a potential sequel to Talk to Me!!! From the terrifying first trailer to the scathing reviews, I knew at some point in my life I was going to watch Cats. It was too much of an anomaly, too high-budget a disaster for me to ignore, I didn’t want to watch it, I HAD to see just how bad it was. And fuck me was this an absolutely terrifying fever dream filled with an uncomfortable amount of drugs, sex and music without having any drugs or sex and too much music. I’m genuinely scarred for having seen it all the way through. Let’s start with the plot. There isn’t any. And I’m not just saying that to be funny, this entire film is 90 minutes of introductions, 10 minutes of actual story and the other 10 minutes is weird panting and gyrating. Here I’ll give you a rundown of what happens; we open with our lead Victoria being abandoned by her owners, she’s introduced to the Jellicle Cats with their Jellicle Ball – and sidenote, they never explain what a Jellicle is and why it’s important to be one despite them saying Jellicle about 587 fucking times in the first five minutes – who take her to see the cats hoping to become the Jellicle choice and live a new life in the fucking sky or something. I swear to Christ, the little plot I can recognise as a story makes me think this is about a fucking suicide cult. From there Victoria meets Rebel Wilson’s hairy cooch, Jason Derulo’s CGI bulge, James Corden’s fat arse, a couple thieving twins who I couldn’t tell if they were related or not because of the fuck me eyes they were flashing at each other, Judi Dench’s old face and Ian McKellen making Meow noises before we actually get to the Jellicle Ball in which the contestants are STILL being introduced since the bad guy – Idris Elba and his unnervingly smooth fur body – has been stealing all the contestants with magic – oh by the way there’s fucking MAGIC in this film, they kinda dropped that on you without warning – so anyone who’s still taking part in the Ball we’ve never fucking seen before, making their musical numbers an exercise in futility because I don’t know them and I don’t want to fucking know them. Those two paragraphs cover around 80% of the story, all this film has is cats introducing themselves through song for an hour and a fucking half and then getting lucky if they have anything to say afterwards. It’s not a plot, it’s a fucking 2 hour montage of people we’ve never seen before and it doesn’t stop, new characters are still being introduced with their own numbers with over half the film already done. The only time it actually works is with Mr Mistoffelees who, despite a fairly low amount of screen-time, has been shown to be a cowardly magician and needs confidence to do Big Magic, that works but it comes so late into the game that it couldn’t save the rest of this train wreck. And before anyone dares defend this film, I know it’s based on a musical and I know it’s a different medium, but Hamilton managed to tell an entire historical story with only singing, this is just cats singing about themselves without a story to give them a reason to sing about themselves. The cast is absolutely stacked with big names who are given nothing to work with, and the ones that have something are the weakest actors in the film, I feel kinda bad for Francesca Hayward who plays Victoria because she’s suppose to be our lead, our surrogate into this bizarre, fucked up world of the Jellicle Cats and she’s given nothing, out of all the speaking parts she has probably the fewest amount of lines, every face she makes has this big wondrous smile about EVERYTHING, no matter how benign, and sure she dances well but in a film where everyone is dancing that doesn’t stand out. This is Hayward’s big theatrical break and she’s the most forgettable element in the film, which ironically might save her career. Out of everyone Victoria meets during the many MANY introductions she has to suffer through, not one of them make it worthwhile to sit through their number. Jason Derolo  - who I just hate in general anyway – sings about how Rum Tum Tugger  is a fussy little cunt then screams for milk, Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer were the thieving twins who looked like they wanted to do a furry version of a Bratty Sis video, and I didn’t know they were twins until writing this review so that just knocks the film even lower for me. There was also a tap dancing train conductor who serves no fucking purpose, Ray WInstone hissing and wondering where the fuck his career has gone and Taylor Swift who even in a film filled with unnecessary sexual energy, gave off too much sexual energy. Seriously man, I got Lola Bunny flashbacks during her number. Worst of the lot was Rebel Wilson and James Corden as Jennyanyfots and Bustopher Jones respectively, I already dislike these two before going into the film and having them both talk the most out of almost any other character was a kick in the fucking dick. Wilson’s introduction was this disturbing piece where she did the most unsexy sexy poses while the camera focussed on her naked hairy body before bringing in singing mice and marching cockroaches with human faces which Jenny proceeds to eat several of when she’s not singing. Corden meanwhile sings for five minutes about being a fat fuck and eating a lot, that’s the entirety of his character, he’s fucking fat, and the fact that both of them are just allowed to skit and makes shitty jokes is simultaneously distracting from the actual plot while adding nothing to the plot either. Both of them were just playing themselves in fur suits and like I said I think both are fucking overdone anyway so I didn’t give a shit about them either way. The only people I see coming out of here unscathed are Ian McKellen and Judi Dench who both have strong enough careers to look past this blip, although Dench’s monologue at the end where she looks at the camera goes on WAY too long about how a cat is not a dog (the fuck?) and every pause makes you think that it’s finally over but no, she keeps fucking going. Jennifer Hudson as Grizabella should also be ok, despite being important to the film she only has three scenes but among those three is her version of the famous ‘Memories’ number which is unironically good, hell I’d say too good for this turd of a film. I’m also hoping that Idris Elba comes out of this unaffected, his villain Macavity is suitably villainous and his motivations generically evil enough – he wants to be the Jellicle Choice because Fuck You I guess – that Elba can work something out with the material but between nobody being able to recognise the most wanted cat in town and his own horrifying nude cat-body, I doubt he’s getting away from this thing clean. Director Tom Hooper has done a few things of note over the last few years, namely his last three films were all Oscar winners and he brought Les Mes to the big screen so I can see why he’s be chosen for this. But holy hell does he fuck this up, this has to go down as one of the biggest fuck-ups of direction of the 21st Century because while Hooper doesn’t do anything technically wrong, nothing he does is done right. Let’s get the big one out of the way; the cats look fucking weird, I knew the cats looked weird, I saw the trailer, I saw the memes, but nothing prepared me for the seeing them in full CGI horror, the first time I saw a Cat-Man clamber down a brick wall, looking like a human being contorting their body into some kind of fucking Cronenberg nightmare with a tail I realised that this was so much worse than I thought it was going to be. It’s the deepest level of the uncanny valley I’ve seen since The Rock in The Mummy Returns and that was 18 fucking years before this, nobody looks human but they don’t look like a cat either, they’re a disgusting hybrid of the two, these vaguely human looking faces pasted onto what looks like skin-tight cat-suits made with actual cat flesh, it NEVER sits right with you. What makes it even more uncomfortable is that there seems to be no rhyme of reason to the clothing, a few cats wear clothing but most of them are nude and some of them even take off their clothes making them nude and I’m left wondering if this is just a nudist colony with lax rules or if everyone is suppose to be naked and we’re just suppose to accept it. I know I shouldn’t be this focussed on naked cat people but I can’t help it, this movie has forces naked cat people into my fucking brain and given me no fucking logic about why they’re naked, hell I haven’t even touched upon the Rebel Wilson scene where she unzips her naked fur-body, as  in literally takes off her skin, to reveal a dance outfit underneath. It’s the tightness as well, I don’t know why they went out of their way to make the cats sexy but it just feels wrong, all the naked cat actors have all their curves pronounced so that every breast, every bulge, every butt covered in fur is on full display but without any form of genitals. Elba gets the worst of it because his fur colour is identical to his skin colour leaving him looking like a fucking Ken Doll with ears but not one person looks good like this. And that’s not even talking about how horny this film is, I heard the stories, I read the reviews that talked about how sexual the film was but it’s not until you’re seeing this cat people twist their bodies together, panting in unison and nuzzle into each other that you have to take a step back and realise that humans doing cat actions is trying way too hard to be sexy whilst not trying to be sexy. The Jellicle Ball is the most horrific example, it’s the hissing, the panting, the Judi Dench hairy leg spread, I honestly couldn’t tell you if the film was trying to be this sexual and went way too far or if it wasn’t trying at all and just came off that way by accident. I haven’t even touched upon the fucking music because I don’t know how to, the visual disaster overpowers the audio so much that I can’t tell if anyone actual sung during this film or not. Ok, over exaggeration, a few songs worked but only a few, the aforementioned Memories hit well and I was fine with the Mr Mistoffelees number but outside of them I really can’t remember any of the songs being any good. The opening introduction to the Jellicle Cats was upbeat I guess, I was too distracted by the CONSTANT use of Jellicle, Jennyanydots was too distracting with the human cockroaches and under-skin dress change for me to even remember what the song was. Tugger and Bustopher were both boring, end of discussion, McKellen’s small number as Gus felt like a lot of build-up for a limp-dick crescendo and Swift’s piece of Macavity trying to big him up almost worked as a villain song if I wasn’t distracted by the complete lack of Idris Elba penis. Before this film the only knowledge I had of Cats was hearing Memories here and there and the rape story from Team America, having now seen this film I know even less about Cats and I don’t want to know anything more about Cats. This is one of the strangest, most confusing, unsettling and fucked up pieces of cinema I’ve ever seen that wasn’t an intentional horror movie, I’ve never seen anything like Cats so 10/10 for uniqueness but just because nobody’s done it before doesn’t mean it’s a good idea and Cats the Movie was not a good idea. There’s no story, all we have is oversexed sexless Cat People introducing themselves for 2 hours before nothing happens and the film ends, nobody looks good, only a couple sound good, the CGI is a mess, the sexiness uncomfortable, the songs forgettable and the whole experience traumatising. I’d say you have to see it just to get the full picture yourself but honestly you’re safer avoiding this. 2/10

É, eu sei o que você está pensando... "como assim???" Apenas me escute Quando o trailer de Cats saiu, eu nao tive interesse nenhum nessa bomba, mas aí um dos meus melhores amigos disse que a gente ia ver no cinema. Eu disse a ele: "-Por que você quer fazer isso??? Esse filme claramente vai ser uma chacota, uma vergonha ridícula" "-Eu sei, você não quer muito conferir esse desastre ao vivo???" E de fato, eu não tive resposta pra essa fala, então, um dia depois do Natal fomos a uma vazia sala de cinema pra assistir um filme que já nasceu morto. E foi umas das experiências mais inesquecíveis de cinema na minha vida. Por ter ido sem nenhuma expectativa de que esse filme pudesse ser bom, eu fui capaz de me divertir bastante sem levar nada a sério. A lógica irrealista (e incoerente) de Cats faz com que literalmente qualquer coisa na cena possa ficar muito engraçada por simplesmente estar ali, é como estar vivenciando um delírio de alta definição. Eu ri absurdamente de várias cenas... mas o que é engraçado mesmo é que eu pude sentir um genuíno charme no meio de toda aquela esquisitice. Eu já reassisti Cats várias vezes e os primeiros 30 minutos realmente me entretém, porque são num ritmo muito dinâmico de música e dança que, se você puder desligar o senso crítico, vai só te carregando nessa gracinha de cenas que não tem absolutamente nenhuma história a não ser gatos cantando. Mais pro meio do filme, realmente começa a ficar enfadonho e cansativo, pois o filme começa a se levar a sério, e quando ele tenta se levar a sério aí é realmente só um desastre mesmo. Tecnicamente, é um filme que de fato merece todo o chapisco. O diretor foi um maníaco que quis fazer caprichos técnicos que dificultaram a vida de todos os profissionais que trabalharam na pós-produção do filme, então esse cara merece mesmo ser avacalhado e ter seu trabalho chamado de o pior filme de todos. E é realmente curioso pensar como nomes tao pesados toparam estar no elenco desse filme. Mas sendo muito sincero, assistir Cats no cinema me trouxe uma epifania de que eu me sentia tão envolvido por aquele filme que não importava de nada que ele fosse um desastre. A sua autenticidade ressoou em mim de uma forma que no final, eu quase me convenci de que era um filme bom. Estou frisando isso para que você entenda que eu não estou defendendo a qualidade de Cats. Estou apenas dizendo que não importa ele ser ruim Às vezes, nós deveríamos só assistir mais filmes ruins e nos entregar à liberdade de não esperar nada do que estamos assistindo. Praticar o exercício de apenas nos entregarmos na experiência de uma obra, e assim percebermos que talvez, um filme ruim também possa te oferecer uma coisa boa. Um filme ruim pode ser engraçado pra caralho. No pior dos casos você ainda vai treinar mais o seu senso crítico. Hoje em dia é tão fácil ser exigente e crítico com tudo, que eu sinto que a coisa mais saudável a se fazer seria realmente, não assistir todo filme do mundo esperando que ele seja bom, mas que seja pelo menos interessante. E isso vai de encontro a uma coisa que eu quero ressaltar: A MAIORIA DAS PESSOAS JULGA ESTE TIPO DE FILME SEM NEM TER SE DADO AO TRABALHO DE VER PRA FALAR MAL. A ESTAS PESSOAS O MEU DESPREZO QUER FALAR MAL???? ASSISTA E TENHA PROPRIEDADE PARA FALAR MAL Pois Cats é um filme horrível mesmo, mas se você se permitir aceitar que ele é horrível, pode talvez conseguir deixar ele te envolver numa experiência lúdica e engraçada, ao fim da qual você vai perceber que ele é um filme ruim de fato, mas nem tanto assim pra criar caso..... Assistam mais filmes ruins, e sejam mais felizes

Saw this in the theater when I picked up the His Name Was Jason DVD, which came with a free movie ticket for the remake. I wonder if sales of that disc counted towards the box office numbers? I only wonder because this thing had a historic second weekend drop-off that basically killed the franchise in the mainstream until the video game came out. I remember seeing trailers for Miss March and the remake of Last House on the Left before the movie started. Even at the time, Miss March felt like it was trying to ride some kind of American Pie wave that had long ago hit the shore and settled back into the seas - no wonder Zach Cregger pretended it didn’t exist when doing the Barbarian press tour. Last House ’s trailer featured a soft girly version of Sweet Child O’ Mine which admittedly felt unique in 2009 compared to the usual Let the Bodies Hit the Floor style nonsense that accompanied horror ads back then. Fast forward to 2026, and the soft-remix trope is one of the top items on my trailer shitlist. You may have noticed I’m not really talking about the movie much, that’s because like all the Platinum Dunes franchise cash-ins of this era, there’s not much to really say. It’s an early 2000’s reboot with that pukey CW Network sheen all over it. To its credit, it was nice to go back to the lake after several entries of goofy nonsense. Trent is one of the all-time douche characters of the entire franchise and Julianna Guill provides some of the best nudity. The kills really should’ve saved this, but aside from the wakeboarding scene, I always struggle to remember any of them even after repeat viewings. If Friday ‘09 (and my accompanying memories at the time of release) is notable for anything, it’s that it was one of the last gasps of the early millennium, and the transition away from things like Drowning Pool, physical media promotions, and raunchy comedies. Watching this feels like a eulogy for the aughts, but as we approach the premiere of a new Crystal Lake series, we know all too well that milking every drop out of a franchise is a timeless endeavor.

I don't think this quite reaches the heights of the best sequels, but it's undeniably a reboot that fundamentally understands the task at hand, and arguably the superior of both Marcus Nispel's 00's horror remakes. Essentially a smooshed-together rendition of the first four original films into a new narrative remix of sorts, after a bit of a ropey opening it skips straight to the good stuff, barrels through the mythology, and gives us Derek Mears' Jason absolutely ruling as a considerably more driven and vicious take on the Hockey Masked killer. I don't really buy the criticisms that it's "too horny", since that promiscuity and lure is kind of part and parcel with the series and its own bizarre detours. The final stretch loses some of the momentum that makes the opening hour such a blast, but the pacing overall is quite relentless, the kills are inventive and nasty, and it's packed with enough of why this series became an institution in the first place. It's a shame it never really spawned anything more, and I look forward to the day we finally get another one of these. Maybe Damien Leone would be a good shout?

Se você tirar o filtro da nostalgia, percebe que este remake entende Sexta-Feira 13 melhor do que boa parte das continuações. Não tenta transformar Jason em um ícone filosófico nem inventar um trauma geracional; só lembra que ele é um cara enorme de máscara cuja principal função é punir gente que acha uma cabana isolada um bom lugar para passar o fim de semana. O Jason do Derek Mears é praticamente o Anton Chigurh dos slashers: paciente, eficiente e inevitável. Enquanto o elenco parece ter saído de um catálogo de comerciais da Abercrombie dos anos 2000, ele faz de Crystal Lake um roguelike: entrou na floresta, morreu, tenta de novo. É engraçado ver como esse filme foi tratado como heresia em 2009 e hoje parece um dos remakes de terror mais honestos da época. Depois de uma década de "terror elevado", às vezes tudo o que eu quero é um sujeito de 2 metros distribuindo machadadas sem precisar representar um trauma intergeracional. Cinema? Talvez não. Entretenimento? Com certeza. E, convenhamos, se você assiste Sexta-Feira 13 esperando a complexidade de Persona, o problema nunca foi o filme.

Joker: Folie a Deux Review: Da Vinci pissing on the Mona Lisa ____________________________________________ "Arthur Fleck is dead.       Long live the Joker." ____________________________________________ 👍: Soundtrack/Sounds: 10/10 Plot/Concept: 6.2/10 Pacing: 7.1/10 Characters: 6.3/10 Emotion: 7.2/10 Cinematography: 10/10 Casting: 9/10 Acting: 9.5/10 Ending: 9.3/10 Overall: 🍿74/90🍿 Joker: Folie à Deux has a lot more good things than people give it credit for. Joaquin Phoenix gives another incredible performance and carries every scene with intensity. I also enjoyed all of the songs , and the soundtrack and sound design create a unique mood. The visuals are beautiful , with grey but yet bright colours that make Gotham look perfect. The scene where Two-Face is born was one of my favourites . And the overall court sequence is excellent. I also liked the ending . I know most people hate it, but I thought it fit the story well. In my opinion, this film is still very overhated. The Message: Joker: Folie à Deux shows how society can turn a broken person into a symbol they never wanted to become. Arthur is no longer seen as a human being with fears, but as the Joker , an idea that people project their own anger onto. The film questions whether people truly care about justice or if they simply enjoy watching chaos. Do we become who we really are or who everyone expects us to be. Arthur struggles between being himself and living up to the Joker . The ending suggests that ideas can survive even when the people cannot. symbols are often more powerful than people, and once society creates a legend , it becomes almost impossible to forget, no matter how much someone changes. ____________________________________________ 👎: Joker: Folie à Deux has a lot of problems. The biggest one is that almost nothing happens. The story barely moves forward , and around 70% of the film feels wasted because there is almost no real progress from beginning to end. The direction is bland, and the overall screenplay is weak. I enjoyed the songs themselves, but the musical numbers often don't fit the story and become exhausting after a while. Good music alone isn't enough to carry such a thin plot. Harley Quinn was also disappointing because she barely does anything important. She had a lot of potential , but the screenplay gives her very little to give , making her feel completely unnecessary. I know the film is overhated , but it's still a pretty mid film . To make things even worse, I watched it at 2 a.m. , so I even lost sleep for it. ____________________________________________ Overall: Joker: Folie à Deux is a weak ass film , but it's still massively overhated. It has some genuinely great aspects , especially the acting, visuals, and music, but they're overshadowed by an unfocused story, bland direction, and wasted potential. The flaws are simply much bigger than the strengths, making it an average experience. Rating by Greatness: ⭐✨ Rating: ⭐⭐ ```````````````

Joker: Folie à Deux nos envuelve ya no en un descenso a la locura, como lo fue la primera, sino en un acompañamiento de este personaje durante su estancia en el reclusorio y en el juicio por los crímenes que vimos en la cinta anterior. Personalmente, considero que esta película, o al menos la historia elegida para contar esta secuela, es innecesaria. No aporta nada realmente nuevo, no desarrolla al personaje —que ya estaba perfectamente construido en la primera entrega— y la coprotagonista, que debería tener mucho peso al tratarse de Harley Quinn, no alimenta la historia como se esperaba. La elección del género musical para esta entrega creo que tenía mucho potencial. La forma en que los números musicales se integran a la cinta, como una representación de la locura dentro de la mente del Joker, funciona bastante bien. Sin embargo, la falta de un guion sólido termina afectando considerablemente esta decisión de género. En general, es una película que, si nunca hubiera existido, no habría pasado absolutamente nada. Incluso creo que mucha gente habría preferido que jamás se hiciera antes que ver cómo fueron desdibujando poco a poco todo lo que construyeron con tanta fuerza en la primera. Aun así, rescato su banda sonora y una fotografía muy cuidada e inteligentemente realizada. Visto En HBO Max

Co written by Scott Silver (The Mod Squad, 8 Mile, The Fighter, Joker, The Finest Hours)  and Todd Phillips and directed by Todd Phillips (Joker, Road Trip, Starsky & Hutch (2004), The Hangover, The Hangover Part II, The Hangover Part III, War Dogs, A Star is Born, Due Date), 'Joker: Folie à Deux' explores the genesis of an ideology born from the violence of a world fuelled by disdain. Phillips continues painting a viscerally dark, painful picture of a man seemingly dismantled by the machinery of law, order and social justice, yet reassembled by the flickering embers of love for a woman captivated by his public enigma. Although 'Joker: File à Deux' weaves musicality into the narrative, this film loses nothing when leading viewers through the protagonists inner workings, and with some excellent performances producing a memorable experience, this is a sequel to be embraced, not disregarded. In closing, 'Joker: Folie à Deux' rests comfortably beside its predecessor, and while a sad, and at times, harrowing portrayal of a truly "tortured" soul, this title will endure multiple, impactful rewatches, which says far more than the critics and naysayer’s who rejected and reviled it's message upon release.

critique, Napoléon – Director’s Cut (2023, Ridley Scott) J’avais découvert Napoléon au cinéma en 2023, et honnêtement, je n’avais pas tellement apprécié le moment. J’étais ressorti assez déçu, avec le sentiment que Ridley Scott passait complètement à côté de son sujet. Je viens enfin de voir la Director’s Cut, et je dois reconnaître une chose : je la trouve meilleure que la version sortie en salles. Les scènes supplémentaires apportent enfin un peu plus de respiration au récit, mais surtout elles développent davantage la relation entre Napoléon et Joséphine. C’est probablement ce qui manquait le plus dans la version cinéma. On comprend mieux leur dépendance affective, leurs tensions et la manière dont leur histoire influence le reste du film. Malgré tout, je reste persuadé que ces ajouts ne suffisent pas à transformer le film en grande fresque historique. Mon principal problème reste le même : je n’ai jamais réussi à m’attacher à ce Napoléon. Joaquin Phoenix est un immense acteur, mais ici je trouve que son interprétation ne fonctionne pas totalement sur moi. Le personnage paraît souvent distant, presque passif, et j’ai parfois eu du mal à retrouver le stratège, le chef militaire ou l’homme politique qui a profondément marqué l’histoire de la France et de l’Europe. Politiquement, c’est aussi ce qui me laisse sur ma faim. Napoléon est une figure complexe, à la fois héritier de la Révolution française et fondateur d’un Empire autoritaire. Le film effleure ces contradictions sans vraiment les explorer. J’aurais aimé qu’il s’intéresse davantage à son héritage politique, à ses réformes, à son rapport au pouvoir ou encore à l’impact immense de ses guerres sur l’Europe. Au final, beaucoup de ces enjeux restent en arrière-plan. Je trouve aussi que le récit manque parfois d’équilibre. Certaines batailles sont expédiées alors qu’elles auraient mérité davantage de temps, tandis que d’autres passages s’étirent sans toujours apporter quelque chose au personnage. En revanche, il y a des choses que je ne peux pas lui enlever. Les costumes sont magnifiques. Et surtout, j’ai beaucoup aimé la photographie. C’est assez paradoxal parce que je n’aime pas particulièrement le film, mais certaines images sont vraiment superbes. Ridley Scott conserve ce talent pour composer des cadres élégants et donner une véritable ampleur à certaines séquences. Visuellement, il y a plusieurs plans qui resteront gravés dans ma mémoire. Les batailles possèdent également une vraie puissance de mise en scène. Même si elles ne sont pas toutes développées comme je l’aurais souhaité, Scott reste un immense réalisateur lorsqu’il s’agit de filmer le chaos, les mouvements de troupes et la violence de la guerre. Au final, cette Director’s Cut améliore clairement le film. Mais pour moi, elle ne règle pas ses principaux problèmes. Je continue de penser que Napoléon est l’un des films les plus faibles de la filmographie de Ridley Scott. Quand on connaît ce qu’il est capable de faire avec Alien, Blade Runner, Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Kingdom of Heaven ou The Last Duel, j’attendais beaucoup plus d’un personnage aussi fascinant que Napoléon Bonaparte. Je suis heureux d’avoir revu cette nouvelle version. Mais je ne pense pas que j’y reviendrai une troisième fois.

‘ France… Army… Joséphine .’ These are widely cited as the final words of Napoleon Bonaparte, encapsulating the three most important things that drove his 51 years of life. Ridley Scott’s 2023 Epic Historical Drama Napoleon feels like the culmination of two centuries of British propaganda; which reduces one of history’s most complex figures into a bumbling, pathetic character who’s only drive is his love for his wife to the point it comes off as a total mischaracterisation of the man. Despite my criticism of Napoleon’s characterisation Joaquin Phoenix’s performance is excellent and perfectly captures the character Scott intended to create. The portrayal of Napoleon as an insecure and emotionally immature man who lashes out at those around him and is only driven by having an heir to secure his imperial dynasty left me actively rooting against him at all times and sympathising with Joséphine. Vanessa Kirby’s performance of Joséphine rivals, if not overshadows that of her co-star. She brought a sense of warmth, struggle, and humanity to the screen. This makes Joséphine feel much more compelling than Napoleon and I found myself vividly enjoying her scenes; while having to suppress the fact the on-screen relationship’s historical accuracy is to be debated. Kirby’s performances was one of the only parts of the film I enjoyed as I felt it had decent emotional weight and focus compared to the other parts of the film. Scott’s attempt to encompass 22 years of the film’s namesakes’ life leads to many major moments in his military and political career are rushed through with little to no historical context or reduced to defining moments in the film created to impress and not inform. Moments such as the French Invasion of Egypt serve only to include notable monuments such as the Sphinx and the Giza Pyramids. Additionally, Napoleon’s eventual desertion of the campaign in order to attempt to seize the opportunity to gain power in the shadow of the French Revolution is instead used to further bolster the romance plot that plagues the film. Conflicts such as The Siege of Toulon , The Battle of the Three Emperors , and The Battle of Waterloo excel in being large eye-catching set-pieces with even those who are not interested in military history will find captivating. However, those who are fascinated in military history; myself included will find ourselves yelling at Scott to include what made those battles so important to the magnitude they are still studied today. I applaud Scott for attempting to create a film on one of history’s most fascinating and decisive figures; however the film fails to fulfil what an audience wishes to see in a two hour feature on Napoleon. Viewers wish to see the story of how an outsider from the Corsican gentry who was dismissed due to prejudice, uses the chaos France was in to become an Emperor. The Napoleonic Wars should have been the focal point of this film, however Scott creates an historical epic that is more focused on being a romance with hints of grandiose set-pieces with the intent to appeal to a large audience. Ultimately this leads to a film that appeals to no-one and is instead carried by the historical name associated to it and the performances of Phoenix and Kirby . As many grievances as I have with this film I would still recommend it if you are able to ignore the mischaracterisations and historical gaps. I understand that general audience may be able to ignore these due to not having enough knowledge on the time period or simply not caring, however as someone who’s always been captivated by the time period I simply could not.

I'm a big history buff, and this movie was painful both in historical context, and as a movie. I heard from some people that it was bad, and yeah, it is. I watched the directors cut, it was 3 1/2 hours of wasted time. The story is very inaccurate and focused too much on the least interesting things about Nepoleon's life, like parts of his relationship with his first wife Josephine, even when the battles happened and are shown, there's a time skip and don't get enough screen time. This movie completely omitted many battles, many events, and even many of the politics that Nepoleon took part in, like they omitted The Battle of the Nations, The Pininsular War, the fall of the Holy Roman Empire, which was a big deal at the time because the Holy Roman Empire had existed for a thousand years at that point. Both The Battle of the Nations and The Pininsular War also played a big role in Nepoleon's downfall, and both were some of the bloodiest events in the Nepoleonic Wars. If I go further with the historical inaccuracies, we'd be here all day, but it got so much wrong and even completely made things up. Despite the directors cut being 3 1/2 hours, it isn't enough to cover Nepoleon's life because of how much he did throughout his career as a soldier, general, consult, and emperor. On top of all that, this movie is boring,  like so boring, it made Nepoleon Bonaparte, one of the most interesting military generals in history, boring, that is an accomplishment. The effects were very good, the CGI, practical effects, the costumes were accurate to the time, the sets, the cinematography, and overall production quality was good. This movie cost about $200 million, and the production clearly shows. However the editing can at times be jarring, even the directors cut. The score was good, I really liked some of the tracks. Oh god, the acting was bad. Joaquin Phoenix was a horrible choice for Nepoleon, his acting didn't have the chops and he had some weird line deliveries. Everyone else was boring and dull, the only exception was Vanessa Kirby as Josephine, she looked and acted like she was trying, it wasn't much but she had the best proformance in the movie. In conclusion, Ridley Scott's Nepoleon is a god awful biopic, it doesn't cover everything about the titular historical figure, and what it does show is overshadowed by the inaccuracies and the fact that it's boring. The cherry on top was Ridley Scott's response to the criticisms from historians, he literally said and I quote "Were you there? No. So, shut the fuck up!" He wasn't there either, so what's he talking about? When French critics called the movie anti-french propaganda, which it kinda is, Scott said that the French hate themselves. What an asshole! If you are a history buff, don't watch this movie. 2/10

As a huge Napoleon fan, I was really excited to watch this movie, and I honestly had pretty high expectations. The costumes were probably my favorite part. They looked beautiful, were mostly historically accurate, and I loved how they recreated so many scenes from famous paintings. Those moments really made it feel like history had come to life.What disappointed me was the story. I really wish they had shown more of Napoleon’s childhood and his rise to power because I think that would have made him feel like a much more complex and sympathetic character. Instead, the movie jumps around a lot and never really lets you understand who he was as a person.It also felt stuck somewhere between a documentary and a historical drama. It wasn’t accurate enough to work as a documentary since so many scenes and events were clearly imagined or changed, but at the same time it wasn’t entertaining enough to make up for those changes. I kept waiting to become emotionally invested, but it never really happened. It looks impressive, but I left feeling like it had missed the chance to tell the incredible story of one of history’s most fascinating people.

I had sensed that I likely wouldn't be watching Napoleon twice, so I decided to watch the Director's Cut straightaway. What can I say, three stars just would have felt too generous for how completely uninvested I was after the first two hours and before Waterloo came. There is certainly merit in seeing this production staged at such an epic scale, and quite a bit of Napoleon is striking to look at in terms of what's on screen, but not in terms of how it looks. Overall, everything here just looks too clean, too digital and intangible for the battle images to move me in any meaningful way, even though they deserve to be praised from the position of technical accomplishment. By the dialogue and Joaquín Phoenix's performance you can certainly tell that Scott's film is openly mocking Napoleon the man, and making you question how a whole country could have been so enamored with him, but looking at today's tyrants and others in history they somehow always manage to sway considerable masses for their greedy and cruel purposes. Begrudgingly, the film also shows Napoleon's military successes, but still finds ways to show him either weak in them or cruel like in the battle of Austerlitz, and certainly singling out the losses his side sustained as ever increasing and ever more disastrous. A really exhausting watch and a far cry from Scott's own similar output.

I'm truly torn and fustrated with this. It's somewhere 3-3.5 for me and very hard to decide. It's fitting Ridley Scott did this, like so many of his films in between his masterpieces it leaves audiences divided. There are parts I think that are great. The production design is great, the winter ice lake battle scene was really good and the best part of the film, Phoenix & Kirby aren't bad together and have their moments, and it never is incoherent. It makes perfect sense and is easy enough to follow along with a deep dive into his relationship with his wife which is arguably the biggest aspect the film focuses on even more so than his battle victories, governing, childhood, relationship with his kids, friends, allies, or return from exile.  He's a fasinating figure and the film does keep an interest for me up until the final 40 minutes or so. The problem here is this probably needs anoth hour or hour thirty minutes to truly encompass everything needed for one of histories most fasinating figures. But also I feel it needs to scale back the focus on his wife. It's literally half the damn film. There needs to be more about his governance, his allies, going into the inner workings of his battle style, his friends and allies and making them as interesting as him. Acting isn't bad thanks to Kirby & Phoenix having their moments. But everyone else just blends in and is forgettable and at times it's too emotioness and wooden. The direction isn't bad either but i reminds me of Spielberg's post A.I. style which I'm not the biggest fan of. Editing and pacing is alright and everything else is half decent. The middle of the movie is the best part. But where this drops the ball for me is how they handled his invasion of Russia and his return to Waterloo. It just felt like it didn't even really dive into the inner working or politics of what happened to lead up to it. If you don't know anything about Napoleon or the Wars of this time I truly can't see how someone would understand what was happening or why. But they choose to continue to focus on his wife and the new wife which really made me baffled. It just doesn't provide enough background or clear motivation on the why's and also showing how he made France into the the envy of the world. And it just made me lose interest and it felt repetitive in a sense too because I knew what was coming. More battles and more drama with the wife which is exactly what I got for the fourth or fifth time. Again nothing is broken here and it does a serviceable enough job I guess. Abba sung about Waterloo in under 3 minutes whereas, for Ridley Scott, his tale of that particular battle, and the life of Napoleon, is closer to 3 hours with an even longer, supposedly 4-hour version coming to AppleTV+. Enough with the facetiousness, Scott’s film of this titanic (but, ironically, pint-sized) figure unfortunately isn’t quite the definite article. Cramming the life of the Emperor, his myriad battles and the ongoing political circumstances, both in France and Europe at the time, into one film was always going to incur a long and unwieldy runtime. Scott does pretty well to keep proceedings clear and moving forward briskly but, because of this approach, a few spots of the history get muddled and you’re left with an interesting and broad overview, albeit one lacking true depth. Scott’s focus is more on the man himself and it works as a character study. On equal footing with the fighting is Napoleon’s relationship with his wife Josephine and it is in these scenes that we get our true glimpse into the man and the true brilliance of Joaquin Phoenix’s portrayal (excellent, as always, and bound to be awards-nominated.) Phoenix tows the line perfectly between showing the stern stoicism of the commander and the vulnerable insecurities of the man. It’s an unbiased and honest portrayal and it’s interesting to speculate and delve beyond just a timeline of events. However, despite attempts to lighten the mood at points with a spot of humour or an original take on the period drama concept, it suffers a little from fustiness and those bright spots only serve to show what this film potentially could have been under different circumstances. It feels like it can’t quite decide what to be and this scattershot nature lets it down. Those more speculative, intimate scenes of Napoleon and Josephine therefore stand as the film’s heart, beyond the wider historical context and scenes of war. It’s also, sadly, very difficult to follow what’s going on in those battle sequences. Great credit must go to all involved for staging such grand scenes but, unfortunately, all bar one suffer from some sort of debilitating factor: too dark, too fast in the edit, too confusing. The Battle of Austerlitz is the one true triumph here and is a sequence to place up there with cinematic large-scale battle scenes. It’s another example where the film shows what it could have been, only fuelling the frustration further. Sadly, Napoleon is just a teensy bit stale and a teensy bit boring. Too unforgivable adjectives in a film of this scale and with a figure of this much interest and importance at its centre (and also from the director of Gladiator.) Hopefully, the longer cut will prove to be the one but a little Swedish-pop, Midas-touch originality is needed here. ⭐️⭐️⭐️

Also I saw the transition between monarchy and the napoleonian/republic regime. It was a good role played by Joaquin Phoenix but not as good as in the Gladiator, that was a hard role to play. There was a thing which I didn't like of this movie, and that is that it was presented in a quiet fast pace, by this I mean the movie wanted to present almost all the political activity of Napoleon in 3 hours, but it was shown in a rapid manner and some events were suddenly happening without knowing how you got there. Now there is a common question whether Napoleon Bonaparte is considered to be a negative character throughout the French history. Well, I don't think that's true until the moment he became corrupted by his own will and powers. It is good to have a nationalist spirit for your country, to want to fight for it, to strengthen it, to protect it, to make it great, but not in an excessive way. Napoleon was completely obsessed that he even sacrificed his love and marriage for France. He loved France, and this is what every leader should do, but there should also be a balance. Not at least, I really liked how was the movie filmed, the frames, the images, they were incredible!

Obsession es un ejercicio sobre la fijación emocional y el deterioro mental. Tiene una puesta en escena sobria, que deja que la incomodidad crezca sin necesidad de exagerar nada. Lo que más funciona es cómo construye tensión desde lo cotidiano. Puede que no sea un corto que busque impresionar visualmente, pero sí deja un mensaje claro de cómo aquello que nos consume puede dañar a quienes nos rodean. Como primer intento, se siente valioso porque ya muestra intención y una búsqueda de identidad. Gracias al director por presentarme este proyecto.

Amazing camera work, and a well thought out concept from Jackson Treadway I felt moved by this short film. in the span of 2 minutes, i felt the obsession and frustration of the protagonist, and through a creative choice of lens and filters, i was transported to a raw, gritty perspective on obsession and drive to succeed Amazing job, looking forward to more short films 👍 Jackson Treadway

Obsession | A Wildly Inventive Horror Spin on Love, Possession, and Personal Space Curry Barker’s Obsession takes a familiar romcom fantasy an awkward guy wishing his crush would love him back, and twists it into something deeply unsettling, darkly funny, and surprisingly sharp. Built on clever writing rather than scale, the film reimagines obsessive affection through grounded horror, where every scene, detail, and escalation serves a purpose. The storytelling constantly flips ordinary gestures of love into disturbing scenarios, creating tension without relying on conventional horror tricks. Michael Johnston convincingly captures the insecurity and panic of the protagonist, while Inde Navarrette is phenomenal in a role that shifts from warmth to terrifying emotional volatility. With inventive visual storytelling, precise atmosphere-building, and a script that finds horror in the collapse of emotional boundaries, Obsession feels refreshingly original. Bottom Line: A creative and confident approach that has been successfully delivered as a smart, unsettling and darkly hilarious horror flick.

Some people love Rollercoasters, or jumping out of planes for a rush or adrenaline; I watch horror films because I hate heights. The last three horror films I watched were Caveat, Oddity and Together; all three made me feel uncomfortable and creeped out. Together more than anything, I started watching it cuddling with my boyfriend, but by the end of the film, I didn't want him anywhere near me for at least 48 hours. But horror films lately have been missing something, something that I longed for. None of them scared me; all of them had a predictable plot, predictable characters, and predictable scares. Until my friend and I saw Obsession at the cinema on Wednesday. I could tell no one in the viewing was going to take it seriously, but we had hope from it being the first 18+ rated horror in a while. It was terrifying. The plot was amazing, and the acting was award-worthy, especially Inde Navarrette; she was absolutely brilliant, and I hope this projects her into more roles. I would love to see her in more horror films for sure. The scares and psychological turmoil were insaneee (in a good way), and you could never predict what was coming next. Even if you've seen clips or audio online and assume you know what it's about, you really don't. They all take you by surprise. I do believe it is more psychological for women to watch, so I suggest if you're a woman, go with your bestie/girlfriend, but if you have a good man, go with him, and he should understand why it's so insane. My friend and I are enthusiastic horror fans, and Obsession was so refreshing because it scared us to the point we left the cinema with our hearts racing and hands shaking.
